entries.question: Who were the sons of David born in Hebron?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 3:2-5 lists David's six sons born in Hebron as Amnon, Chileab, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, and Ithream. 1 Chronicles 3:1-4 lists them as Amnon, Daniel, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, and Ithream. The lists agree on five of six, but the second son's name differs.
entries.commentary:
This is the same contradiction as entry 239, expanded to the full list. The two lists agree completely on first, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth — Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, Ithream — and on the mothers. They diverge only on the second son's name (Chileab vs. Daniel). The mother (Abigail of Nabal/Carmelite) and the birth-order position match.

The apologetic move and the critical move are the same as in entry 239. Dual-name (Archer, Keil-Delitzsch) vs. textual variation (McCarter, Anderson, Japhet, Klein). The LXX manuscript tradition for 2 Samuel 3:3 preserves multiple readings (Daluyah, Daluiah, Chileab), which McCarter takes as evidence that the name was unstable in early transmission.

Where this entry adds something over the previous one is the comparative scope. The fact that the two lists agree on five of six entries shows they share a common source — they are not independent attestations. The Chronicler is using Samuel as a source and reproducing the list. The single point of divergence is therefore not two independent traditions disagreeing but a transmission variant at one point in a shared list. That actually strengthens the textual-corruption explanation: if the Chronicler had Samuel in front of him and reproduced the list with one name change, the change is either deliberate harmonization-of-an-unfamiliar-name or a copyist substitution. Neither one supports the dual-name hypothesis. Why would the Chronicler change a name but keep everything else identical, unless his Samuel manuscript already read "Daniel" or unless he is deliberately substituting?

The parsimonious account is that early transmission of the name varied (Chileab and Daniel both attested in different manuscript streams), the MT of Samuel preserved one form, the MT of Chronicles preserved the other, and there is no underlying historical fact about a dual name. Take your pick — but the dual-name hypothesis requires an unattested cultural detail (David's son had two names) while the textual variation hypothesis is supported by actual surviving manuscript variants.

entries.question: Was Solomon David's second or fourth son by Bathsheba?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 12 narrates the birth of Solomon as the immediate replacement child after the death of Bathsheba's first son, implying Solomon is her second son. 1 Chronicles 3:5 lists four sons born to David by Bathshua/Bathsheba in Jerusalem — Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon — making Solomon her fourth, not her second.
entries.commentary:
The Samuel narrative is built as a tight moral parable. Nathan confronts David, the first child of the adultery dies, David comforts Bathsheba, and she immediately bears Solomon. The text doesn't pause to insert two intermediate brothers between the dead infant and Solomon. That's the whole rhetorical point — the LORD took one child and gave back another, and the one He gave back is the heir. 2 Samuel 12 is a theodicy story, not a birth registry.

The Chronicler then comes along centuries later, working from his own genealogical sources, and gives a flat list of four Jerusalem sons by Bathshua daughter of Ammiel: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon. That's not a casual aside — Chronicles is obsessed with genealogies, and the order is deliberate. Solomon is listed fourth. The Chronicler is not telling the Bathsheba-Uriah story (he scrubs the adultery entirely), so he has no narrative reason to compress.

The harmonization apologists reach for is the standard one: 2 Samuel 12 never explicitly says Solomon was the second-born, it just narrates his birth without mentioning siblings. Technically true. But that requires reading 2 Samuel as a deliberately incomplete birth notice, with Shimea, Shobab, and Nathan slotted in silently between verses 24 and 25 — and it requires explaining why the narrator would say "she bare a son, and he called his name Solomon" right after the comfort scene if three other sons had already been born in between. The plain reading of Samuel and the genealogy in Chronicles point in different directions.

The parsimonious explanation is that the two authors are working from different traditions with different purposes. Samuel is a court narrative reshaped around David's sin and restoration. Chronicles is a post-exilic priestly recalculation of the royal line. Neither author was trying to coordinate with the other.

entries.question: Where did God kill Uzza?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 6:6 locates Uzzah's death at "Nachon's threshingfloor." 1 Chronicles 13:9 locates the same event at "the threshingfloor of Chidon." Both texts describe the identical incident — Uzzah steadying the ark, the oxen stumbling, God striking him dead — but they name the location differently.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the most transparent Samuel-Chronicles divergences in the text. Same scene, same actor, same outcome, two different threshing-floor names. The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 6:6 reads Nodab/Nodan, and the textual apparatus shows scribes were already struggling with this name in antiquity. The Hebrew of Samuel has Nachon (nakon, which can also be read as a participle meaning "prepared"); Chronicles has Chidon (kidon, which can mean "javelin" or "destruction"). Either both are corrupted forms of a lost original, or the Chronicler is working from a different tradition entirely.

The standard apologetic move is to claim the threshing-floor had two names — owned by Nachon, sometimes called Chidon — or that one is a personal name and the other is a place-feature. Keil and Delitzsch made exactly this move in the nineteenth century. The problem is that nothing in either text supports this. Neither narrator hints at a dual name. The text in Samuel says "Nachon's threshingfloor." The text in Chronicles says "the threshingfloor of Chidon." The harmonizer is inventing a tradition neither author preserved to rescue a contradiction neither author noticed.

The critical reading is simpler. The Chronicler is working from Samuel as a base text but had access to variant traditions, or he is correcting what he found in his Vorlage. The textual history of Samuel is notoriously messy — the Qumran fragments (4QSam-a) show that the MT of Samuel has suffered significant corruption, and McCarter's Anchor Bible volume documents dozens of cases where Chronicles preserves an older or different reading. This is a name-variant, not a divinely-coordinated travel itinerary.

Nothing theologically heavy rides on the location. But "Where did this happen?" is exactly the kind of question two reliable witnesses should agree on, and these two don't.

entries.question: How many horsemen did David take?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 8:4 says David captured from Hadadezer a thousand chariots and seven hundred horsemen. 1 Chronicles 18:4 reports the identical event as a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen — a tenfold discrepancy in the cavalry count.
entries.commentary:
These are parallel reports of the same campaign against Hadadezer king of Zobah. Same king defeated, same chariot count, but the horsemen number jumps from 700 in Samuel to 7,000 in Chronicles. That's not a rounding difference. That's an order of magnitude.

The textual data here actually helps narrow the problem. The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 8:4 reads seven thousand, agreeing with Chronicles against the Hebrew MT. The Dead Sea Scrolls fragment 4QSam-a, while damaged at this verse, generally aligns with the LXX tradition in similar cases. The most parsimonious reading is that the Hebrew text of 2 Samuel has suffered a scribal omission of an "alep" (the abbreviation for "thousand") and the original number was 7,000, which Chronicles and the LXX preserve. That makes this a textual corruption in MT Samuel rather than a doctrinal contradiction.

This is the move apologists generally also make — Gleason Archer goes there in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, and so do most evangelical commentators. Fine. But notice what the apologist concession amounts to: the received Hebrew Bible, the text presented as inerrant in countless pulpits, contains a transmission error that changes the number by a factor of ten. The "contradiction" gets resolved by admitting that one of the canonical texts is wrong. That's a perfectly reasonable historical-critical conclusion. It's also a problem for any doctrine of preserved inerrancy.

The contradiction is real at the level of the received canonical text. The resolution requires either accepting textual corruption (which undermines inerrancy in the form most lay believers hold it) or doing the harmonization gymnastics where the 700 are some elite subset of the 7,000, which neither text actually says.

entries.question: How many men did David kill?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 10:18 reports David killed 700 men in chariots and 40,000 horsemen of the Arameans/Syrians. 1 Chronicles 19:18 reports the same battle as 7,000 men in chariots and 40,000 footmen — both the chariot men and the type of the 40,000 troops differ.
entries.commentary:
Two discrepancies, same battle. First, the chariot-men jump from 700 in Samuel to 7,000 in Chronicles — same kind of factor-of-ten variance as the 2 Samuel 8 / 1 Chronicles 18 horsemen number. Second, and more interesting, the 40,000 are horsemen in Samuel but footmen in Chronicles. Cavalry versus infantry is not a rounding error; that's a different kind of force.

On the 700 versus 7,000 question, the same textual-corruption analysis applies as in entry 243. The MT of 2 Samuel is unstable, the LXX often agrees with Chronicles, and the most economical explanation is a missing "alep" in Samuel. The horsemen-versus-footmen swap is harder. The Hebrew words are different — parashim (horsemen) versus raglim (footmen) — so this isn't a simple letter-confusion. Either the Chronicler had a different source, or he is deliberately editing the type of troop to fit his theological picture of Davidic warfare, or one of the manuscripts has corruption at the word level rather than just the number.

The harmonization attempts here get strained. Keil and Delitzsch suggest the 40,000 were mixed forces and the two authors counted them differently — Samuel emphasized the cavalry component, Chronicles the infantry component. That's possible in principle but unsupported by either text. Neither narrator says "of these, some were cavalry and some infantry." Each gives a single number with a single descriptor. The harmonization requires importing information neither text contains.

The critical reading: parallel battle reports from two different post-exilic compositions working with overlapping but non-identical source traditions, plus textual corruption in MT Samuel. Some Bible Difficulties authors (Archer) acknowledge the textual problem; the broader inerrancy claim then requires defending the autographs while admitting the received text is corrupt.

entries.question: When did Absalom rebel against David?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 15:7 reports Absalom's rebellion begins "after forty years." 2 Samuel 5:4 states David reigned only forty years total. If 15:7 is read as forty years into David's reign, the rebellion comes at the very end of his life — but the rebellion narrative is followed by years of additional reign and the eventual succession of Solomon, which is internally inconsistent.
entries.commentary:
This one is an internal Samuel problem, not a Samuel-versus-Chronicles problem. 2 Samuel 5:4 sets David's total reign at 40 years. 2 Samuel 15:7 then says "after forty years" Absalom hatched his Hebron coup. If "forty years" counts from the start of David's reign, then Absalom rebelled in the last year, which leaves no room for everything 2 Samuel 16-24 and 1 Kings 1-2 describes happening afterward — David's flight, the Mahanaim period, the return, the Sheba revolt, the census, the threshing-floor purchase, the succession struggle.

The Septuagint and the Syriac Peshitta and a few Hebrew manuscripts read "after four years" rather than "after forty" at 2 Samuel 15:7. Most critical scholars, including McCarter in the Anchor Bible volume, take "four" as the original reading and "forty" as a textual corruption — probably a scribe assimilating to the round number forty that appears so often in Samuel. Even Josephus, in Antiquities 7.196, knows the tradition as "four years."

So the apologetic move here is actually the same as the critical one: the MT "forty" is a textual error and the original was "four." Where critic and apologist part ways is what to do with that admission. The critic says: this is normal for ancient texts, MT Samuel is full of these corruptions, the Bible is a human document. The apologist says: the autographs were inerrant, the transmission introduced errors, but the underlying text is recoverable. Either way, you can't get out of this contradiction without conceding that one of the canonical texts has an error.

There is also a harmonization that tries to read "forty years" as counting from David's anointing by Samuel rather than from the start of his Hebron reign, but the chronology still doesn't work out cleanly, and nothing in the text signals such a counting scheme.

entries.question: Who was Amasa's father?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 17:25 identifies Amasa's father as Ithra "an Israelite." 1 Chronicles 2:17 identifies him as Jether "the Ishmaelite." The discrepancy is both in the form of the name and, more importantly, in the ethnicity.
entries.commentary:
Two questions here. First, is the name Ithra or Jether? That one is easy — they are variant spellings of the same Hebrew name (yeter / yitra), and this kind of variation is normal in Hebrew transmission. Not a real contradiction at the name level.

The ethnicity is the real problem. Samuel says yisre'eli, "Israelite." Chronicles says yishme'eli, "Ishmaelite." The Hebrew words differ by a single letter and a vowel pattern, so a scribal error in one direction or the other is mechanically plausible. But which is the corruption? The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 17:25 reads "Jezreelite" (yizre'eli) in some manuscripts and "Ishmaelite" in others. McCarter and most critical commentators reconstruct the original as "Ishmaelite," matching Chronicles — partly because identifying David's nephew's father as a plain "Israelite" is uninformative (everyone in the narrative is Israelite, so calling Ithra one tells the reader nothing), and partly because Chronicles tends to preserve older readings against MT Samuel in many cases.

The harmonization is to say Ithra was an Ishmaelite by birth who resided among Israelites and adopted Israelite identity, or that the two terms designate different things — birth versus residency. That's not impossible. But it's a story neither text actually tells. Neither narrator says "He was born Ishmaelite but lived as Israelite." Each gives one designation flatly.

The simplest reading is that the Samuel text suffered a single-letter corruption from yishme'eli to yisre'eli — the kind of mistake medieval scribes made constantly — and Chronicles preserves the older reading. That makes Amasa half-Ishmaelite, which is actually theologically interesting given that he becomes David's army commander. A non-Israelite at the top of the Davidic military hierarchy is the kind of detail the Chronicler had little motivation to invent.

entries.question: How many sons did Absalom have?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 14:27 says three sons were born to Absalom. 2 Samuel 18:18 has Absalom himself saying he has no son to keep his name in remembrance, which is why he set up a memorial pillar. Both statements appear in the same book about the same person.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in Samuel. Chapter 14 reports three sons by name (well, by number — only the daughter Tamar is named). Chapter 18 has Absalom explaining the existence of his memorial pillar by saying he has no son to keep his name alive. Both can't be straightforwardly true of the same man at the same time.

The traditional harmonization is that Absalom's three sons died young. Childhood mortality in the ancient Near East was brutal, the argument goes — three boys could easily have died before reaching the age where they'd carry on a father's name. The pillar in 2 Samuel 18:18 is then explained as something Absalom set up after the deaths of his sons, when he realized his name would die with him. The explicit "sons died young" reading is a rabbinic harmonization; Josephus in Antiquities 7.243 simply records Absalom's stated motivation for the pillar ("if his children should perish, his name would remain by that pillar") without asserting that the sons actually died.

The problem with that reading is that the text never says it. 2 Samuel 14:27 reports the births as a piece of straightforward biographical data, no death notice attached. 2 Samuel 18:18 doesn't say "after his sons died." The harmonization works by importing a death event neither narrator mentioned and which the chronology of Absalom's relatively short adult life makes tight to fit.

The other harmonization is that 14:27 refers to sons who would later be born — that is, Absalom's projected future progeny — but the verb is past-tense Hebrew narrative consecutive, not a prediction. The critical reading is that Samuel is composite, drawing on multiple source traditions, and the contradiction reflects the editor's failure to harmonize a notice about Absalom's family in one source with a notice about the pillar in another. The pillar in 18:18 is the older, more weight-bearing tradition — it explains a real monument the original audience would have known. The three-sons notice in 14:27 is biographical fill that doesn't connect to anything else in the narrative.

entries.question: How many children did Michal (David's first wife) have?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 6:23 states Michal had no child to the day of her death. 2 Samuel 21:8 refers to "the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul" who were handed over to the Gibeonites to be impaled.
entries.commentary:
Within the same book of Samuel, Michal is described both as childless to her death and as the mother of five sons who get executed by the Gibeonites. The five sons in 21:8 are usually attributed to Adriel the Meholathite as their father.

The textual situation actually favors the harmonization here, but in a way that makes a different problem visible. A number of Hebrew manuscripts, the Lucianic Greek tradition, the Syriac Peshitta, and a substantial chunk of critical scholarship read "Merab" rather than "Michal" at 2 Samuel 21:8. Merab was Michal's older sister, and 1 Samuel 18:19 explicitly says Merab was given to Adriel the Meholathite as a wife. So the five sons of Adriel the Meholathite are Merab's sons, not Michal's, and the MT "Michal" at 21:8 is widely treated as a scribal error — probably a copyist's mind slipping from the more famous sister to the less famous one.

This is the rare case where the apologetic move (it's a scribal slip, the text originally said Merab) lines up cleanly with the critical conclusion. McCarter, Klein, Tsumura, and most modern translations note this in their apparatus. The NRSV and NIV emend to Merab in the text or footnote. The KJV preserves the MT "Michal," which is why the SAB and other contradiction lists pick this one up — they're working from the received Masoretic Hebrew.

What the harmonization concedes, again, is that the canonical Hebrew text has an error here that all the modern scholarly editions have to fix from the versions. The contradiction is real at the level of the MT. It dissolves only by acknowledging textual corruption. That's a perfectly defensible scholarly position, but it's not consistent with strong preservation-of-the-Hebrew-text inerrancy claims.

entries.question: Who did Elhanan kill?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim killed Goliath the Gittite — the same Goliath whom 1 Samuel 17 credits David with killing. 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath. The KJV inserts "the brother of" into 2 Samuel 21:19 to harmonize, but the Hebrew has no such phrase.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the most famous and embarrassing harmonizations in the entire King James tradition. The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:19 says, in word-for-word literal translation: "And Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam." Not "the brother of Goliath." Just Goliath. The KJV translators added "the brother of" in italics — they at least had the integrity to mark it as not in the text — but the Hebrew Bible says Elhanan killed Goliath.

This directly contradicts 1 Samuel 17, where David kills Goliath in the celebrated duel. Two different killers, same victim, both narratives presented as historical fact. The most parsimonious historical reconstruction is that the older tradition, preserved in 2 Samuel 21:19, credits Elhanan — a relatively obscure warrior — with killing Goliath. The later, more famous David-and-Goliath story in 1 Samuel 17 is a literary expansion that transfers the kill from the obscure soldier to the rising king. Many critical scholars treat the David version as theologically motivated reattribution.

The Chronicler, working with both Samuel narratives in front of him, sees the contradiction and fixes it. 1 Chronicles 20:5 reads: "Elhanan son of Jair struck down Lahmi, brother of Goliath the Gittite." The Chronicler invents (or preserves a tradition of) a previously unmentioned brother Lahmi to absorb Elhanan's kill, leaving David as the unique slayer of Goliath. The Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles 20:5 even gives this brother the name Lahmi (lakhmi), which looks suspiciously like a fragment of beth-hallakhmi ("the Bethlehemite") from 2 Samuel 21:19 that the Chronicler reanalyzed as a personal name.

The critical consensus, including McCarter, Klein, and Tsumura, is that 2 Samuel 21:19 is the older, embarrassing tradition, and that both the KJV's italicized insertion and the Chronicler's "Lahmi the brother" are scribal/editorial attempts to rescue David's exclusive claim to the Goliath kill. This is a textbook case of how harmonization gets baked into the canonical text itself.

entries.question: Did David sin?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 22:21-25 has David claiming the LORD rewarded him according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands. 1 Kings 15:5 says David did right "all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah." 2 Samuel 24:10 and 1 Chronicles 21:8 have David confessing he sinned greatly in numbering the people. So at least three answers exist within the canon: none, one (Uriah), and at least two (Uriah plus the census).
entries.commentary:
The three texts answer the same question — did David sin? — in three incompatible ways. 2 Samuel 22, paralleled in Psalm 18, is a victory psalm where David sings about his own righteousness in absolute terms: clean hands, righteousness, no departure from God's statutes. Read at face value, this is David saying he hasn't sinned. 1 Kings 15:5 is a deuteronomistic editorial summary that gives the qualified answer — David was righteous except in the Uriah affair. 2 Samuel 24:10 and 1 Chronicles 21:8 introduce a second confessed sin, the census.

The standard harmonization is that 2 Samuel 22 is a piece of liturgical poetry written before the Bathsheba and census incidents, or that David is speaking comparatively (righteous compared to Saul), or that "cleanness of hands" refers to specific contexts (his treatment of Saul) rather than his entire moral record. There is something to the comparative-righteousness reading — the psalm is set in the context of David's deliverance from his enemies, and the immediate referent is probably his behavior toward Saul. But the language is unqualified: "according to my righteousness ... according to the cleanness of my hands ... in his eye sight." Not "compared to Saul." Not "in this matter." The psalmist's voice is making a categorical claim.

1 Kings 15:5 then explicitly carves out the Uriah exception — which means the Deuteronomist who wrote that summary considered the Uriah affair David's only sin. He didn't say "except for Uriah and the census." He said only Uriah. So either the Deuteronomist didn't know the census story, didn't count it as a sin, or considered Uriah categorically worse. 2 Samuel 24 and 1 Chronicles 21 both treat the census as a confessed sin, so the canon as a whole records at least two sins, but 1 Kings 15:5 reports only one.

The critical reading is that these texts come from different hands with different agendas. The Deuteronomistic Historian's summary in 1 Kings 15:5 is designed to make David the standard against which later Judean kings are measured, and the Uriah affair is the only stain he allows on the standard. Different authors, different evaluations, no editorial coordination.

The SAB also lists the second reference as "2 Samuel:22:21" with an extra colon — that's a formatting artifact in the scrape, not a real verse citation problem; the verse exists and the language is as quoted.

entries.question: What were David's last words?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 23:1-7 explicitly introduces a poetic oracle as "the last words of David," a Spirit-inspired psalm of righteous kingship. 1 Kings 2:1-9 records David's deathbed instructions to Solomon, which are largely a list of people to settle scores with — Joab, Shimei — sometimes called the "hit list." Both texts present themselves as David's final pronouncements.
entries.commentary:
2 Samuel 23 frames the oracle with the explicit superscription, "These are the last words of David," and gives the king an inspired meditation on the just ruler under God. 1 Kings 2 then opens with David charging Solomon at the threshold of death and works through a series of unfinished business items, ending with Joab and Shimei. Both can't literally be the last words.

The harmonization is that 2 Samuel 23:1 means "David's last inspired poetic utterance" rather than "the last words he spoke before dying." That's not implausible. The Hebrew phrase divre david ha-akharonim can be read as "David's later words" or "David's last poetic words," especially since 2 Samuel 23 is clearly a literary unit of inspired speech rather than a deathbed scene. 1 Kings 2 then provides the historical-narrative deathbed and there is no contradiction at the level of strict chronology.

Fine. But notice what gets lost in that move. 2 Samuel 23:2 says "The Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue." The chapter is presented as the prophetically inspired David, full stop, in a position of climactic moral and theological summation. 1 Kings 2 then has the same David, at the actual end of his life, telling Solomon to make sure Joab's gray head goes down to the grave with blood. The two pictures of David are in significant tension even if they aren't literally the same speech-event. The Deuteronomistic Historian who edited 1 Kings 2 is presenting a David who dies giving Solomon a kill order. The compiler of 2 Samuel 23 is presenting a David whose inspired finale is a meditation on the righteous king.

Most critical scholars treat 2 Samuel 23:1-7 as a late insertion into the Samuel scroll — an editorial addition placed near the end of David's narrative to give him a final poetic-prophetic word. 1 Kings 2 is the older, harder-edged tradition of David's actual deathbed. The contradiction isn't only chronological. It's about which David the canon wants you to remember: the inspired psalmist or the dying king settling scores. The canon preserves both, side by side, without choosing.

entries.question: How many mighty men did David have?
entries.summary: Both citations point to the same passage, 2 Samuel 23:8-39, which concludes by claiming "thirty and seven in all." When the names in the preceding list are tallied, the count comes out to thirty-six, not thirty-seven. The contradiction is between the summary number the text gives itself and the actual list of names the text supplies.
entries.commentary:
This is a self-counting problem inside a single chapter. 2 Samuel 23 lists David's elite warriors in tiers — the three, the second three, and the thirty — and then sums everything up as "thirty-seven in all." Count the names that survive in the MT and you get thirty-six. Count them in the Chronicles parallel (1 Chronicles 11:10-47) and the list is longer because the Chronicler keeps adding names, but the totaling problem is specific to Samuel.

The standard harmonization is that one or more names dropped out of the list during transmission. That is almost certainly correct. The MT of 2 Samuel 23 shows visible textual damage — multiple names with corrupted spellings, a couple of place-names that look garbled — and the Chronicler's parallel list, written later, preserves additional names. A name lost in scribal copying is consistent with the summary number originally matching the original list. McCarter's Anchor Bible volume reconstructs which name probably dropped out.

Fine — and again, that's the apologetic and the critical reading agreeing on the mechanism. What it doesn't get you out of is the conclusion that the received Hebrew text contains a textual error, since the named list and the summary total don't agree. You can blame the scribes, but the canonical text disagrees with itself in front of you. The contradiction is internal to a single chapter and visible to anyone who counts.

This is a textbook case of how the contradiction-list genre works: it's not always about deep theological mismatches. Sometimes it's about the Bible failing at basic arithmetic on a list it just gave you. The fact that the resolution requires positing scribal corruption — rather than denying the discrepancy — is itself the answer to whether the Bible's numbers are reliably preserved.

entries.question: How many valiant men drew the sword in Israel and Judah as counted by Joab?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 24:9 gives the census totals as 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah. 1 Chronicles 21:5 gives the same census as 1,100,000 for Israel and 470,000 for Judah. Both Israel and Judah numbers disagree between the two reports.
entries.commentary:
Same census, taken by the same Joab on the order of the same David, with both Israel and Judah numbers in disagreement. 800,000 versus 1,100,000 for Israel — a 300,000-man difference. 500,000 versus 470,000 for Judah — a 30,000-man difference. The Chronicler inflates the Israel number and trims the Judah number.

The standard harmonization is that the two texts count differently. Maybe Samuel counts only Israel's standing army while Chronicles includes some additional category. Maybe Judah in Samuel includes Levi and Benjamin while Chronicles excludes them. Maybe one count is at a different stage of Joab's tour. Keil and Delitzsch run through several variations of this in their Samuel commentary. Each version requires inventing a counting distinction the text doesn't mention.

The other standard move is to call the numbers symbolic. The figures are too round, too large, and too convenient to be literal demographic data — Israel and Judah combined couldn't have fielded more than a million men in the tenth century BCE. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman's work on the actual demographic capacity of Iron Age Israel and Judah puts the population in the low hundreds of thousands total, soldiers and civilians combined. So both numbers are inflated, and the question is just which inflation the author chose. That is a real critical insight but it doesn't resolve the contradiction at the level of the text — both authors present their numbers as straight historical reportage.

The parsimonious reading is that the Chronicler is working from Samuel as a source but using different round figures, possibly to fit his theological emphasis on the magnitude of David's force or to align with other genealogical numbers in his own composition. The numbers in both Samuel and Chronicles are best understood as literary-theological constructions rather than census records. The contradiction is between two non-historical constructions, but the contradiction is still there: each text tells you the soldiers were counted, and each gives a different count.

entries.question: How many years of famine?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 24:13 has the prophet Gad offering David seven years of famine as one of three punishment options. 1 Chronicles 21:11-12 has Gad offering the same David three years of famine as one of three punishment options. Same prophet, same king, same divine message, two different numbers.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest small contradictions in the Samuel-Chronicles parallel set. Same prophetic encounter, same three-option ultimatum, but the duration of the famine option is different in each text. Seven years in Samuel, three years in Chronicles.

The textual evidence cuts toward Chronicles. The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 24:13 reads three years, agreeing with 1 Chronicles 21:11-12 against the MT of Samuel. Most critical commentators reconstruct "three" as the original, since it also matches the pattern of the other two options — three months of pursuit, three days of plague. A neat three-three-three structure is rhetorically tighter and is the form preserved in both LXX Samuel and MT Chronicles.

The standard harmonization is that the seven in MT Samuel refers to the full famine cycle including years already underway. Some commentators point to the three-year famine of 2 Samuel 21:1, suggest a one-year recovery, and then propose three more years offered by Gad as a continuation — adding to seven. That requires connecting two unconnected famine narratives separated by several chapters and importing a recovery year nobody mentions. It's the kind of harmonization that, even if true, would be invisible to any reader without a calculator and a chart.

The simpler explanation: the MT of 2 Samuel reads seven, the LXX of 2 Samuel reads three, the MT of 1 Chronicles reads three, and the original was three. MT Samuel has suffered a scribal corruption — possibly assimilation to the seven-year famine in Genesis 41 or the seven-year cycle elsewhere. This is one more case where the harmonizer and the critic agree that one of the canonical texts has an error; they disagree only on what to do about it.

entries.question: How much did David pay for the threshing floor?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 24:24 says David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. 1 Chronicles 21:25 says David gave six hundred shekels of gold for the place. The price differs in both quantity (50 vs 600) and metal (silver vs gold).
entries.commentary:
Same purchase, same buyer, same seller, two completely different prices. 50 shekels of silver buys you a small piece of agricultural equipment in the ancient Near East. 600 shekels of gold buys you a kingdom. The disparity isn't a rounding issue — it's an order of magnitude in unit count plus a switch in metal.

The standard harmonization splits the purchase. The argument runs: 2 Samuel 24:24 describes David buying just the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, while 1 Chronicles 21:25 describes David buying "the place" — meaning the entire site of the future Temple, a much larger plot — for six hundred shekels of gold. Two different transactions, two different parcels of land. Keil and Delitzsch make this argument; modern evangelical commentators repeat it.

The problem with this harmonization is that both texts present a single transaction, in the same narrative flow, with the same purpose: David sacrifices on the threshing floor immediately after the purchase. Neither text breaks the purchase into two stages. Neither text says "the small price was for the equipment, the large price was for the larger plot." The harmonization invents a second transaction the text doesn't describe.

The more honest reading is that the Chronicler is inflating the price — and switching to gold — to make the foundation purchase of the Jerusalem Temple site theologically appropriate. Fifty shekels of silver is what a poor man pays for a piece of equipment. Six hundred shekels of gold is what a great king pays for the future site of the holy of holies. The Chronicler, writing in the post-exilic period when the Temple is central to Judahite identity, has every reason to upgrade David's contribution to the Temple project. Japhet, Klein, and Knoppers all read this as a deliberate Chronistic enhancement.

The contradiction is real, and the most parsimonious explanation is that the Chronicler is editorializing — making the founding transaction grander to match the theological weight he assigns to the site. Both numbers can't be literal; one is the price actually preserved in the older tradition (50 silver in Samuel) and the other is a theologically motivated inflation.

entries.question: Was Solomon alone when he sacrificed 1000 burnt offerings at Gibeon?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 3:4 describes Solomon going to Gibeon and offering a thousand burnt offerings, with no mention of any congregation accompanying him. 2 Chronicles 1:3-6 describes the same sacrifice as a public event with "all the congregation" of Israel going up with Solomon to the high place at Gibeon.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 3:4 says "And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there ... a thousand burnt offerings did Solomon offer upon that altar." Singular subject, no congregation mentioned. 2 Chronicles 1:3-6 says "Solomon, and all the congregation with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon ... And Solomon ... offered a thousand burnt offerings upon it." Same sacrifice, same number, same place, but in 2 Chronicles the entire congregation is present.

The standard harmonization is the argument from silence: 1 Kings doesn't say Solomon was alone, it just focuses on Solomon. The congregation may well have been there, the Deuteronomistic Historian just didn't think it was worth mentioning. That's defensible up to a point. 1 Kings 3 is built around Solomon's personal encounter with God in the dream — the narrative spotlight is on the king individually, and the writer streamlines accordingly. The narrative compression isn't a denial that others were present.

But consider the SAB's framing of the question: "Was Solomon alone when he sacrificed?" If we take the question strictly, then yes, 1 Kings presents the sacrifice as Solomon's personal act and 2 Chronicles presents it as a national assembly. The harmonization works at the level of "not technically excluded by silence," but it doesn't work at the level of "both texts present the same picture." 2 Chronicles 1 is doing something the Deuteronomistic Historian didn't do — making Solomon's sacrifice a corporate, congregational event consistent with the Chronicler's theology of all Israel worshiping together.

Japhet and Klein both note this is a typical Chronistic move: the Chronicler regularly transforms private royal acts into public assemblies of all Israel. David moving the ark, Solomon's enthronement, Hezekiah's Passover — the Chronicler scales them up. So the contradiction isn't a strict logical impossibility, but it's a substantive divergence in how the two writers reconstruct the same event. The plain reading of 1 Kings 3 doesn't include the congregation; 2 Chronicles 1 explicitly does.

The more interesting question is theological: 1 Kings 3 is also slightly embarrassed about Solomon sacrificing at a high place, since the Deuteronomistic theology disapproves of high places. The narrator explains it away by noting the Temple wasn't built yet. The Chronicler has even more to explain, and one way he handles it is to make the Gibeon visit a fully authorized national act with the entire congregation present.

entries.question: Who was the greatest: Jesus or Solomon?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 3:12 has God telling Solomon that none would arise like him in wisdom, before or after. Matthew 3:11 has John the Baptist declaring Jesus mightier than himself. Matthew 11:11 and Luke 7:28 have Jesus declaring John the Baptist the greatest born of women, but then immediately saying the least in the kingdom is greater than John. Matthew 18:1-4 has Jesus saying the greatest in the kingdom is whoever humbles themselves like a child. The texts give multiple incompatible answers about who is greatest.
entries.commentary:
This entry packs at least four different "greatest" claims into one question, and they aren't all addressing the same axis. Solomon is called greatest in wisdom. Jesus is mightier than John. John is greatest born of women. The least in the kingdom is greater than John. The humble like a child is greatest in the kingdom. These aren't all rankings on the same scale.

The Solomon claim in 1 Kings 3:12 is specifically about wisdom — "a wise and an understanding heart" — and the surrounding narrative treats Solomon's exceptional wisdom as a divine gift unmatched before or since. The harmonization here is that "none like thee" specifically refers to the gift of administrative and judicial wisdom, not to overall greatness. That is exegetically defensible. The text is about wisdom, not about cosmic ranking.

The John the Baptist material is where the harmonization gets harder. Matthew 11:11 and Luke 7:28 both say John is the greatest of those born of women — categorical language, no qualifier — and then immediately say the least in the kingdom is greater than John. So the same sentence both elevates John above all humans and demotes him below the kingdom's lowest member. The standard harmonization is that John is greatest in the old covenant order and the kingdom is a new order on a different scale. That works as theology but it doesn't make "greatest" mean the same thing across the two halves of the verse. The Greek meizon is used in both clauses with no semantic shift signaled.

Matthew 18:1-4 then gives a third answer: the greatest in the kingdom is whoever humbles themselves like a child. So the kingdom's hierarchy is defined by humility, which means there's no fixed person who is "the greatest" — it's whoever embodies the disposition. That's a different conceptual framework from "X is greater than Y" rankings.

This question is less a clean logical contradiction and more an aggregation of different greatness-claims in different contexts. The honest critical reading is that the New Testament texts in particular are doing something rhetorical: John is the greatest under the old order, but the new order — the kingdom — flips the ranking, making humility the qualifier. The contradiction with Solomon is solvable by noting the different scales (wisdom vs. covenant-status vs. mighty-deeds). The internal Matthean tension between "John is greatest" and "the least is greater than John" is harder to dissolve without conceding that the saying contains an intentional paradox.

entries.question: How many stalls did Solomon have?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 4:26 says Solomon had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots. 2 Chronicles 9:25 says he had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots. The numbers differ by a factor of ten.
entries.commentary:
Same king, same stables, two numbers, factor-of-ten difference. Either Solomon kept ten times more horse-stalls than archaeologists could ever support, or one of the texts has a transmission error.

The textual answer is straightforward. The Septuagint of 1 Kings 4:26 actually reads four thousand, agreeing with 2 Chronicles 9:25 against the Hebrew MT. The number 40,000 in the MT of Kings is widely recognized as a textual corruption — probably an accidental doubling of the letter or a scribal slip. The cross-comparison with 1 Kings 10:26, which lists Solomon's chariots at 1,400, makes 4,000 stalls (a roughly three-to-one stall-to-chariot ratio) far more militarily plausible than 40,000 stalls for 1,400 chariots — that would be nearly thirty stalls per chariot, which makes no operational sense.

The apologetic position generally concedes this: it's a textual error in MT Kings, the LXX and Chronicles preserve the original. Archer says so directly in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties. Most modern evangelical translations footnote the issue. So once again, the contradiction at the level of the received MT is real, and the resolution requires admitting the canonical Hebrew text has a copying error. That's the same pattern we keep seeing in this batch.

On the historical-archaeological side, neither number is plausible for tenth-century Israel. The so-called "Solomonic stables" at Megiddo turn out to be ninth-century structures built under the Omride dynasty, and they're storehouses, not stables, in any case. Solomon's grand cavalry-and-chariot operation is largely a literary construction. So the contradiction is between two literary numbers, with the smaller one (4,000) being the more textually defensible reading.

entries.question: Who was Heman's father?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 4:31 calls Heman a "son of Mahol" along with Ethan, Chalcol, and Darda. 1 Chronicles 2:6 lists Heman among the sons of Zerah. 1 Chronicles 6:33 and 1 Chronicles 15:17 identify Heman the singer as the son of Joel. Three different fathers for Heman: Mahol, Zerah, and Joel.
entries.commentary:
This one is partly resolvable by realizing the texts may not all be talking about the same Heman. The Heman of 1 Kings 4:31 is paired with Ethan, Chalcol, and Darda as legendary wise men. The Heman of 1 Chronicles 6:33 and 15:17 is a Levitical singer in the temple choir, son of Joel. These are likely two different Hemans — the wisdom-tradition figure and the temple musician.

That takes care of part of the problem but not all of it. 1 Chronicles 2:6 lists Heman, Ethan, Chalcol, and Dara/Darda as sons of Zerah — which is the same set of names as 1 Kings 4:31 except for Zimri added at the front. So the Chronicler is clearly working with the same wisdom-tradition Heman as Kings, but identifies the father as Zerah rather than Mahol. "Mahol" in 1 Kings 4:31 may be a profession-term (mahol means "dance" or "musical instrument") rather than a personal name — the phrase bene mahol could mean "sons of dance" or "members of the dance/music guild," in which case the wisdom-Heman is identified by his guild rather than his biological father. That's a possible harmonization for the Kings-Chronicles wisdom-figure conflict. The Septuagint of 1 Kings 4:31 actually transliterates Mahol as a name, suggesting the LXX translators read it that way; later commentators have read it both ways.

If we accept that mahol is a guild-name and Zerah is the actual lineage, then 1 Kings 4:31 and 1 Chronicles 2:6 can be reconciled. The Joel-father references in 1 Chronicles 6:33 and 15:17 are a different Heman — the Levite musician — and there is no contradiction with the wisdom-Heman.

That said, the harmonization is partly an inference. The SAB question collapses what may be two different men into one, but it also points to a real ambiguity in how the texts name Heman's lineage. The cleanest reading: two Hemans, the wisdom-figure (Zerah lineage, also called "sons of Mahol" in his guild capacity) and the Levite musician (Joel lineage). The contradiction is mostly an artifact of treating two different people as one.
